'''Aspisoma''' (as-pi-sō′mä̤), ''n.'' [NL., irreg. < Gr. ἀσπίς, a shield, + σῶμα, body.] A genus of South American fireflies, of the family ''Telephoridæ'', belonging to the malacodermatous division of pentamerous ''Coleoptera''. ''A. lineatum'' is the common firefly of the Amazon region.

'''Asplanchna''' (as-plangk′nä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄσπλαγχνος, without bowels, < ἀ- priv. + σπλάγχνα, bowels.] A genus of free ''Rotifera'', having a rounded sac-like body, devoid of appendages, and possessing neither anus nor intestine, whence the name. The genus is typical of the family ''Asplanchnidæ''.

'''asplanchnic''' (as-plangk′nik), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἄσπλαγχνος, without bowels (see ''Asplanchna''), + ''-ic''.] Having no intestine or alimentary canal; anenterous.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|Aspila|342|asprino}}</noinclude>of moths, family ''Noctuidæ'', founded by Guénée. {{smaller|The larvæ are smooth, soft leaf-feeders. ''A. virescens''
is a beautiful moth, with olivaceous fore wings, marked with three distinct pale lines, relieved by coincident deeper shades.}} '''2.''' A genus of coleopterous insects.

[[File:century v01 p0368 c1f1.png|center|223px]]
{{c|{{smaller|''Aspila virescens.'' (Natural size.)}}}}

'''aspine†''' (as′pin or -pīn), ''a.''   [Irreg. < ''asp''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ine''<sup>1</sup>.]   Of or pertaining to an asp; snaky: as, “''aspine'' venom,” ''Quarles.''

'''aspirant''' (a-spīr′ant or as′pi-ra̤nt), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< F. ''aspirant'', a candidate (prop. ppr.), < L. ''aspiran(t-)s'', ppr. of ''aspirare'' (> F. ''aspirer''), aspire: see ''aspire.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' One who aspires; one who seeks advancement, elevation, or preference.
{{smaller block|Our young ''aspirant'' to the name and honours of an English senator.
{{right|''Bp. Hurd.''}}}}
{{smaller block|“Beauty and extraordinary goodness” were her dowry; and she was claimed by four separate ''aspirants.''
{{right|''Bancroft'', Hist. U. S., I. 196.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Aspiring; ambitious: as, “our ''aspirant'' souls,” ''Mrs. Browning.''—'''2.''' Ascending; mounting up: as, ''aspirant'' flames. [Rare in both uses.]

'''aspirate''' (as′pi-rāt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''aspirated'', ppr. ''aspirating''.   [< L. ''aspiratus'', pp. of ''aspirare'', give the ''h''-sound to, breathe or blow upon: see ''aspire.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To pronounce with a breathing or an audible emission of breath; pronounce with such a sound as that of the letter ''h'': as, we ''aspirate'' the words ''horse'' and ''house'', but not ''hour'' and ''honor''; cockneys often ''aspirate'' words beginning with a vowel.
{{smaller block|Such mutes as were originally ''aspirated''—that is to say, had an audible bit of an ''h'' pronounced after them.
{{right|''Whitney'', Lang. and Study of Lang., p. 93.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove by aspiration.—'''Aspirating winnowing-machine''', {{smaller|one in which aspiration or suction is used instead of a blast. See ''winnower''.}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be uttered with an aspirate or strong breathing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Where a vowel ends a word, the next begins either with a consonant, or what is its equivalent; for our ''w'' and ''h'' ''aspirate''. {{right|''Dryden''.}}}}

'''aspirate''' (as′pi-rāt), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''aspiratus'', pp.: see the verb.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Pronounced with the aspirate or rough breathing; pronounced with the ''h''-sound, or with a strong emission of breath.
{{smaller block|The Zend often showing an ''aspirate'' mute where the Sanskrit has the unaspirate, and vice versâ.
{{right|''J. Hadley'', Essays, p. 172.}}}}
{{smaller block|They are not ''aspirate'', ''i. e.'', with such an aspiration as ''h''.
{{right|''Holder'', Elem. of Speech.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' An aspirated sound, or a sound like our ''h''; a sound with which the ''h''-sound is combined, or which corresponds historically to a sound of this nature: thus, the Sanskrit ''kh'', ''gh'', ''bh'', etc., and the Greek ''ch'', ''th'', ''ph'' (χ, θ, φ) are called ''aspirates'', as are also the English ''f'', ''th'', which are more properly called breathings or spirants; also, a character or combination of characters representing a sound thus described, as the letter ''h'', the Greek rough breathing, etc.

'''aspirated''' (as′pi-rā-ted), ''p. a.'' Same as ''aspirate.''

'''aspiration''' (as-pi-rā′shọn), ''n.''   [< L. ''aspiratio''(''n''-), a breathing upon, aspiration of a sound, the aspirate letter ''h'', < ''aspirare'': see ''aspirate'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of aspirating or breathing; a breath.
{{smaller block|Fanned with continued breezes, and gentle ''aspirations'' of wind.
{{right|''Steele'', Englishman, No. 26.}}}}
'''2.''' An aspirated sound; a phonetic breathing.
{{smaller block|The ''h'', the pure ''aspiration'', is an expulsion of flatus through the position of the adjacent letter, whether vowel, semivowel, or nasal.
{{right|''Whitney'', Life and Growth of Lang., p. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Latin grammarian Priscian, about 500 {{sc|a. d.}}, tells us that the sound then expressed by ''f'' was originally signified by ''p'' with an ''aspiration'' (that is, by ''ph'').
{{right|''J. Hadley'', Essays, p. 172.}}}}
'''3.''' The act of aspiring or ardently desiring; an ardent wish or desire, chiefly after what is elevated or spiritual.
{{smaller block|She . . . feels neither inclination to pleasure nor ''aspiration'' after virtue.
{{right|''Johnson'', Rambler, No. 112.}}}}
{{smaller block|All Emerson’s ''aspirations'' were toward greatness of character, greatness of wisdom, nobility of soul.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 928.}}}}
'''4†.''' Aid; inspiration; countenance.
{{smaller block|To God’s honour, . . . without the ''aspiration'' and help of whose especial grace no labours of man can profit. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 357.}}}}

'''5.''' The act of removing a fluid, as pus or serum, from some cavity of the body, by means of a hollow needle or trocar connected with a suction-syringe.—'''6.''' Suction; the act or process of drawing air through (by some method of exhaustion), as opposed to the act or process of forcing it through—that is, to a blast.
{{smaller block|For cleaning grain there are other kinds of apparatus in which the principle of ''aspiration'', or drawing currents of air through the grain, is now extensively employed.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IX. 344.}}}}
='''Syn. 3.''' Longing, yearning.

'''aspirator''' (as′pi-rā-to̤r), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''aspirare'', breathe or blow upon: see ''aspirate'' and ''aspire''.]   '''1.''' An apparatus for creating a vacuum by the action of a moving fluid. {{smaller|A common form is that of a simple vessel filled with water and connected with the receptacle to be drained of air. On permitting the water to escape below, a partial vacuum is formed above it.}} '''2.''' A surgical instrument, consisting of a hollow needle, or trocar, connected with a suction-syringe, used in removing fluids from the cavities of the body.—'''3.''' A form of winnowing-machine employing aspiration instead of a blast. See ''aspiration'', 6.

'''aspiratory''' (a̤-spīr′a̤-tọ̄-ri), ''a.''   [< L. as if *''aspiratorius'', < ''aspirare'', breathe upon: see ''aspirate'' and ''-ory''.]   Pertaining to breathing; suited to the inhaling of air.

'''aspire''' (a̤-spīr′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''aspired'', ppr. ''aspiring''.   [< late ME. ''aspire'', < F. ''aspirer'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''aspirar'' = It. ''aspirare'', < L. ''aspirare'', ''adspirare'', breathe or blow upon, desire to reach, < ''ad'', to, + ''spirare'', breathe, blow: see ''spirit''. Cf. ''conspire'', ''expire'', ''inspire'', ''perspire'', ''respire'', ''suspire'', ''transpire''.]   '''I.'''† ''trans.'' '''1.''' To breathe to or into. {{smaller block|To spreade his beames vpon vs, and ''aspire'' hys breth into vs. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Apol., xlix. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''2.''' To breathe forth or exhale.   ''Shenstone.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose notes the air ''aspire''
Of th’ old Egyptian or the Thracian lyre.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Golden Age Restored.}}}}

'''3.''' To breathe after; seek with eagerness to attain to; long or try to reach; attempt.
{{smaller block|Who dare ''aspire'' this journey? {{right|''Donne'', Poems, p. 184.}}}}

'''4.''' [See II., 2.] To mount or soar to; attain.
{{smaller block|<poem>That gallant spirit hath ''aspir’d'' the clouds.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Come, there was never any great thing yet
''Aspired'', but by violence or fraud.</poem>{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 3.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be eagerly desirous; aim ambitiously, especially at something great or noble; be ambitious: followed by an object with ''to'' or ''after'', or by an infinitive: as, to ''aspire to'' a crown or ''after'' immortality.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Aspiring'' to be gods, if angels fell,
''Aspiring'' to be angels, men rebel.</poem>{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 127.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He ''aspired'' to see
His native Pisa queen and arbitress
Of cities.</poem>{{right|''Bryant'', Knight’s Epitaph.}}}}

'''2.''' [Partly influenced by association with ''spire.''] To rise up as an exhalation, or as smoke or fire; hence, to mount or ascend; tower up or rise high.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose flames ''aspire'',
As thoughts do blow them, higher and higher.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., v. 5, song.}}}}

'''aspire†''' (ạ-spīr′), ''n.''   [< ''aspire, v.'']   Aspiration; ardent wish or desire. {{smaller block|And mock the fondling for his mad ''aspire''. {{right|''Chapman.''}}}}

'''aspirement†''' (a̤-spīr′mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''aspire'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of aspiring; aspiration.
{{smaller block|By which ''aspirement'' she her wings displays.
{{right|''Ant. Brewer'' (?), Lingua, iii. 8.}}}}

'''aspirer''' (a̤-spīr′ėr), ''n.'' One who aspires; an aspirant.

'''aspiring''' (a̤-spīr′ing), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Animated with an ardent desire, as of power, importance, or excellence; ambitious; soaring: as, “''aspiring'' nobles,” ''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., i.
{{smaller block|''Aspiring'' beggary is wretchedness itself.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ere he filled with loves, hopes, longings, this ''aspiring'' heart of man. {{right|''Lowell'', Anti-Apis.}}}}
'''2.''' Rising; towering or soaring.
{{smaller block|To sore destruction dooms the ''aspiring'' wall.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xii. 368.}}}}

'''aspiringly''' (a-spīr′ing-li), ''adv.'' In an aspiring manner; soaringly; ambitiously.

'''aspiringness''' (a-spīr′ing-nes), ''n.'' The state of being aspiring; ambitiousness. [Rare.]

'''aspis''' (as′pis), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἀσπίς, an asp, the Egyptian cobra: see ''asp''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Same as ''asp''<sup>2</sup> or ''aspic''<sup>1</sup>. Also used as a generic term.—'''2.''' [''cap.''] A genus of coleopterous insects.   ''Germar.''—'''3.''' [''cap.''] A genus of lepidopterous insects.   ''Treitschke'', 1829.

'''aspish''' (as′pish), ''a.''   [< ''asp''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ish.'']   Of or pertaining to asps; snaky.   ''N. E. D.''

'''Aspisoma''' (as-pi-sō′mä̤), ''n.''   [NL., irreg. < Gr. ἀσπίς, a shield, + σῶμα, body.]   A genus of South American fireflies, of the family ''Telephoridæ'', belonging to the malacodermatous division of pentamerous ''Coleoptera''. ''A. lineatum'' is the common firefly of the Amazon region.

'''Asplanchna''' (as-plangk′nä̤), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἄσπλαγχνος, without bowels, < ἀ- priv. + σπλάγχνα, bowels.]   A genus of free ''Rotifera'', having a rounded sac-like body, devoid of appendages, and possessing neither anus nor intestine, whence the name. The genus is typical of the family ''Asplanchnidæ''.

'''asplanchnic''' (as-plangk′nik), ''a.''   [< Gr. ἄσπλαγχνος, without bowels (see ''Asplanchna''), + ''-ic''.]   Having no intestine or alimentary canal; anenterous.

'''asplanchnid''' (as-plangk′nid), ''n.'' A rotifer of the family ''Asplanchnidæ''.

'''Asplanchnidæ''' (as-plangk′ni-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Asplanchna'' + ''-idæ''.]   A family of rotifers having the trochal disk rounded, the wreath single and marginal, the trophi incudate, and no intestine, anus, or foot. ''Asplanchna'' is the leading genus.

'''Asplenium''' (as-plē′ni-um), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. ἀσπλήνιον, also σπληνίον, usually ἄσπληνον (> L. ''asplenum''), spleenwort, supposed to be a cure for the spleen, < ἀ- euphonic + σπλήν, spleen: see ''spleen''.]   A genus of ferns characterized by linear or oblong sori lying on the veins (which are free in most species) and obliquely to the costa, the involucre being conformable to the sorus and opening toward the costa when single.
{{smaller block|It is the largest genus of the order (''Filices'') excepting ''Polypodium'', and its species are found in all parts of the world, wherever ferns grow. It includes very varied forms. Many of the species are evergreen, and some are cultivated for their beauty. Among the more common species, generally known as spleenwort, are the lady-fern (''A. Filix-fœmina''), black maidenhair (''A. Trichomanes''), distributed around the globe, wall-rue (''A. Ruta-muraria''), and ebony spleenwort (''A. ebeneum'').}}

'''aspodil†''', ''n.'' An obsolete and corrupt form of ''asphodel'' (''Asphodelus ramosus''). Also ''aspodflower''.   ''Holme'', 1688.

'''asporous''' (a-spō′rus), ''a.''   [< Gr. ἀ- priv. + σπόρος, seed: see ''spore''.]   Without spores; not developing spores.
{{smaller block|In the case of the simplest and most minute Schizomycetes (Micrococcus, etc.) no definite spores have been discovered; any one of the vegetative micrococci may commence a new series of cells by growth and division. We may call these forms ''asporous'', at any rate provisionally.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXI. 404.}}}}

'''asport''' (as-pōrt′), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''asportare'', carry away, < ''abs'', away (see ''ab-''), + ''portare'', carry.]   To carry away; especially, to remove feloniously.   ''N. E. D.'' [Rare.]

'''asportation''' (as-pōr-tā′shon), ''n.''   [< L. ''asportatio(n-)'', a carrying away, < ''asportare'', pp. ''asportatus'': see ''asport''.]   '''1.''' A carrying away or off. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Aubrey, whose “Miscellanies” were published in 1696, had no doubts whatever as to the physical ''asportation'' of the witch. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 115.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''criminal law'', the felonious removal of goods from the place where they were deposited. It may be theft, though the goods be not carried from the house or apartment.

'''aspre†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''asper''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Aspredinæ''' (as-prẹ̄-dī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Aspredo'' + ''-inæ''.]   Same as ''Aspredinina'' or ''Aspredinidæ''.   ''Swainson'', 1839.

'''aspredinid''' (as-pred′i-nid), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Aspredinidæ''.

The skin is either smooth or tuberculous.}}

'''Aspredo''' (as-prē′dō), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''aspredo'', roughness, < ''asper'', rough: see ''asper''<sup>1</sup>.]   A genus of nematognathous fishes, typical of the family ''Aspredinidæ''.

'''asprely†''', ''adv.'' See ''asperly''.

'''aspreness†''', ''n.'' See ''asperness''.
